lessons.title: il pane — bread, and its companions
lessons.gloss: bread — closest to Latin pānis, and the "companion" who shares it

segments.text: il pane ("bread") — and, true to form, Italian keeps it closest to Latin: pānis becomes pane, barely touched. Its root carries the same warm story as the French pain: a companion is one you share bread with.
il pane ("bread") from Latin pānis — masculine, il pane; the plural is i pani.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: bread family

segments.text: companion / company from com- ("with") + pānis — "one you break bread with."

And a purely Italian gem: companatico — the word for "whatever you eat with bread" (cheese, salami, anything on it). The bread is the given; the companatico is what joins it — the same com- + pānis idea, alive in one Italian word.

segments.instruction: "pane becomes companion, companatico" — bread and what joins it

segments.text: Give "bread" with its article. (il pane.) What Latin word, and how much did Italian change it? (pānis — barely: pānis becomes pane.) What does companatico mean, and how does it use the bread-root? ("What you eat with bread" — com- "with" + pānis.) Next: l'acqua and il vino.

lessons.title: l'acqua, il vino — water and wine, close to the source
lessons.gloss: water and wine — acqua kept Latin's whole aqua, where French wore it to eau

segments.text: The Italian table's two drinks — and a neat contrast with French. Where French dissolved Latin aqua into a bare eau ("oh"), Italian kept it almost whole: acqua, with the aqua still ringing in it.

l'acqua ("water") from Latin aqua. Italian barely moved it — it even doubles the sound with -cq- (AH-kwa), holding onto the hard qu that French threw away. Set them side by side: Latin aqua becomes Italian acqua (kept) vs French eau (worn to a vowel). English borrowed the same loud original for aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct. Takes l' before the vowel.
il vino ("wine") from Latin vīnum — clean and close, like everything Italian. The same word travelled into English as wine, and gives vine, vinegar, vintage, vineyard, vinyl. Masculine: il vino.

segments.text: Give "water" and "wine" with articles. (l'acqua, il vino.) How does Italian acqua differ from French eau, from the same aqua? (Italian kept it — even doubling -cq-; French wore it to a single vowel.) Name an English cousin of each. (acqua becomes aquatic/aquarium; vino becomes wine/vinegar.)
